content: Workplace stress refers to the physical and emotional responses that occur when a woman faces demands or pressures at work that exceed her adaptive capacity. Mechanisms of workplace stress in women involve a complex interplay of psychosocial stressors, including job demands, control, social support, and gender-specific challenges such as discrimination or work-family conflict. Physiologically, stress activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and sympathetic nervous system, leading to release of cortisol and catecholamines, which affect cardiovascular, immune, and metabolic functions. Women may experience distinct patterns due to hormonal fluctuations and social roles. Synonyms include occupational stress, job stress, and psychosocial work stress. Workplace stress significantly impacts women's mental health through anxiety, depression, and burnout, and physical health areas like cardiovascular disease risk. It also affects work performance and quality of life. Practical relevance includes designing gender-sensitive stress management interventions, workplace policies, and lifestyle adaptations. Limitations of current evidence include variability in study designs and underrepresentation of diverse female populations. Safety considerations emphasize recognizing stress-related symptoms early and avoiding self-medication with substances. This module provides an evidence-calibrated understanding aimed at women, healthcare providers, and employers to support healthier work environments and individual coping strategies.
